title: Binary Search
definition: Binary search finds a target value in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the range it still has to look in.
explanation:
Start with the whole sorted list and compare the target with the middle element. If they match, you are done. If the target is smaller, it can only be in the left half; if it is larger, it can only be in the right half. Throw the other half away and repeat on what is left.

Every comparison discards half of the remaining candidates, so the number of steps grows with the *logarithm* of the list size. A sorted list of one million items needs at most about 20 comparisons, where a left-to-right scan could need a million.

Two requirements matter: the data must be **sorted**, and you must be able to jump straight to the middle element (arrays, not linked lists). A classic bug is computing the midpoint as `(low + high) / 2`, which can overflow fixed-width integers in languages like Java and C++. Writing `low + (high - low) / 2` avoids it.
whyItMatters: Searching sorted data is everywhere: database indexes, dictionary lookups, `git bisect`, and finding where to insert into a sorted collection. The same halving idea works any time you can ask "is the answer above or below this point?", even when there is no list at all.

examples.title: Iterative
examples.explanation: The search range is items[low..high]. Each loop iteration shrinks it by moving one end past mid. In real Python code, prefer the standard library's bisect module.

examples.title: Iterative
examples.explanation: Same algorithm. JavaScript numbers are doubles, so (low + high) cannot overflow for realistic array sizes, but Math.floor is needed because division is not integer division.

examples.title: Iterative
examples.explanation: With 32-bit ints, low + high can exceed the maximum value on very large arrays, so the midpoint is computed as low + (high - low) / 2. The JDK ships this as Arrays.binarySearch.

examples.title: Iterative
examples.explanation: The same loop over a std::vector. In production C++, std::lower_bound and std::binary_search implement this for you.
